newsitem.title: USA: USDA sees higher corn, soybean acreage, lower wheat.
newsitem.headline: USDA sees higher corn, soybean acreage, lower wheat.

text.p: The Agriculture Department on Tuesday projected higher U.S. corn and soybean acreage this year along with lower wheat acreage.

In official projections that were updated in early February, the department estimated 1997/98 planted corn acreage at 81.0 million acres, up slightly from last year's 79.5 million acres, soybean acreage at 65.3 million acres, up significantly from last year's 64.2 million and wheat acreage at 70.0 million, down from 96/97's level of 75.6 million acres.
The projected soybean acreage would be the highest since the mid-1980s, USDA said in its report released at the department's annual Agricultural Outlook Forum.
USDA said some land unplanted to soft red winter wheat in the mid-south and Midwest is likely to go to soybeans.
Overall, soybean area should be up in the western Corn Belt but down in the eastern Corn Belt and increases are also expected in most other areas including the southeast and Delta.

The 1997/98 corn production was put at 9.560 billion bushels, up from last year's 9.293 billion, soybean production 2.475 billion bushels versus 2.382 billion last year, and 97/98 wheat production was projected at 2.270 billion bushels, compared to 2.282 billion last year.
Grain and soybean stocks at the end of next season were all projected to improve from this year's tight levels.
The 1997/98 corn ending stocks were estimated at 1.249 billion bushels, up from 96/97 levels of 959 million bushels and almost three times greater than 95/96 ending stocks.
The 97/98 soybean ending stocks were pegged at 220 million bushels versus 140 million in 96/97 and 97/98 wheat ending stocks were projected at 554 million bushels versus 474 in 96/97.

USDA projected soybean exports to drop in 1997/98 to 855 million bushels, compared to 96/97's high level of 905 million bushels. The department said global import demand for soybeans will moderate, mainly because of less imports by the EU and China.

The 1997/98 wheat exports were projected to increase slightly to 1.0 billion bushels, up from last year's 950 million. Sharp competition and modest growth in import demand for wheat will keep U.S. exports weak, USDA said.

The department also projected that average crop prices to farmers would decline in 1997/98. USDA projected the average corn price at $2.50 per bushel versus $2.70 in 1996/97, wheat at $3.45 per bushel versus $4.30 in 1996/97, and soybeans at $6.60 per bushel, down from $7.00 in 96/97.
